headlines.title: OpenAI reveals new instances of ‘concerning' AI behavior during testing
headlines.description: OpenAI has disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial intelligence models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated. The AI company also said Wednesday it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called “misalignment,” including where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight. OpenAI’s latest announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns. Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots.” In another instance, an AI “agent” uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user. The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said. “As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research,” OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events. “Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves,” the company said. Artificial intelligence 20 hours ago Artificial intelligence Sep 14 Wednesday’s new cases followed OpenAI’s disclosure in July that its rogue AI system hacked into AI startup Hugging Face. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organizations during testing. AI “agents” are becoming smarter and have become “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia. That’s making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said. OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices. “That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su added.

headlines.title: San Francisco fire station shakeup ordered after ‘derogatory' poster found
headlines.description: A poster mocking several San Francisco firefighters has led to a command shakeup at one of the city’s fire stations, with the department shifting four lieutenants, two captains and three battalion chiefs after the discovery. The poster was found pinned to the wall last month at Fire Station No. 8 on Bluxome Street, according to multiple department sources with knowledge of the incident. The poster featured photographs of several female firefighters and one male firefighter, all of whom were on leave, according to the sources. Across the top were the words, “STRESS…IT’S AN EPIDEMIC!” The bottom read, “Station 8 INVESTIGATES.” At the center was an apparent image of a state hospital sign, with the words “CRIMINALLY INSANE” underlined and an arrow pointing toward one of the firefighters. Another firefighter on leave was mocked for having an allergy to the flame-retardant protective clothing firefighters wear, known as turnout gear. Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter said department commanders spotted the poster on a wall in a common area during a recent visit to the station. Fire Chief Dean Crispin subsequently told a group of female firefighters that the poster was “inappropriate and derogatory,” according to department sources. Crispin also issued a memo to firefighters warning them against workplace harassment. “Upholding a respectful and professional environment is essential to the safety, trust, and integrity of our department,” Crispin wrote earlier this month. The chief declined to discuss the matter, but in a statement, the department said after officials “became aware of potentially inappropriate material posted at a workplace,” they took immediate corrective action. “The San Francisco Fire Department is committed to promoting and maintaining a safe and healthy work environment where every individual is treated with civility, dignity, and respect,” the department said. A department official confirmed that four lieutenants, two captains and three battalion chiefs have been transferred from Station No. 8 in response to the poster. The department said it continues to investigate who was responsible for putting up the poster. Meanwhile, none of the more than two dozen firefighters assigned to the station has been transferred, according to the department.

headlines.title: 1 dead, 2 injured after fishing boat crashes near Golden Gate Bridge
headlines.description: One person died and two others were injured after a fishing boat crashed into rocks and capsized near the Golden Gate Bridge on Thursday morning, according to the San Francisco Police Department. Officers assigned to the SFPD Marine Unit responded around 6:10 a.m. to reports of a 25-foot vessel in distress beneath the north side of the Golden Gate Bridge, within Marin County’s jurisdiction. With assistance from the U.S. Coast Guard Station Golden Gate, SFPD’s Real Time Investigation Center, Southern Marin Fire, the San Francisco Fire Department’s Marine Unit and the Sausalito Fire Department’s Fire Boat Liberty, crews located all three people and provided medical aid, police said. All three were taken to a hospital in Marin County with life-threatening injuries. One of the passengers later died at the hospital despite lifesaving efforts by emergency responders, police said.

headlines.title: Large fire breaks out at vacant warehouse in Alameda
headlines.description: A large fire broke out at a vacant warehouse in Alameda early Thursday morning, according to the Alameda Fire Department. Fire crews responded around 1:15 a.m. to the building on Rainbow Court, near Tower and Orion streets and south of Midway Avenue. The large, multistory vacant building is part of the former Alameda Naval Air Station site. Firefighters have since knocked down the blaze. No injuries were reported. Crews are expected to remain at the scene for several hours. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

headlines.title: Nonprofit launched in honor of animal advocate killed in San Jose triple shooting
headlines.description: A year after her daughter was killed in a triple shooting, a San Jose mother is reclaiming the tragic day and turning it into something positive. Jeannessa Lurie’s loved ones gathered Wednesday at Paul Moore Park to carry out her legacy as an animal advocate and launched “Jeannessa’s Friends,” a nonprofit organization that aims to provide funding, education, and resources to animal rescue groups and low-income pet parents. Lurie, 24, was gunned down at her home last September alongside her roommate, Tarrah Taylor, and her boyfriend, Max Ryan. The alleged gunman, Joseph Vicencio, was Taylor’s boyfriend and is currently behind bars. In her first interview since the killings, Lurie’s mother Jeanna said her daughter confided in her a couple of weeks before the shooting, saying she didn’t like Vicencio and tried getting her roommate away from him. “A really horrible person did a really horrible thing and he took my daughter’s life and he took the lives of Tarrah Taylor and Max Ryan,” Jeanna said. “I didn’t want him to take my life, and I wanted to be inspired by the things my daughter brought to this world in the short time she was here.” San Jose Sep 18, 2025 San Jose Sep 19, 2025

headlines.title: DOJ files lawsuit against San Jose over gun permit fees
headlines.description: The United States Department of Justice is suing the city of San Jose, saying its $1,600 gun permit fee is unconstitutional. San Jose’s gun permit application fee is the highest in the nation. The federal government said charging private individuals that “exorbitant fee” violates the Second Amendment. Feds claim it denies citizens their right to carry firearms for self-defense. NBC Bay Area reached out to San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan for comment but did not immediately hear back. The San Jose Police Department was also named in the lawsuit. The department does not comment on pending litigation.

headlines.title: Petaluma high school student arrested after allegedly bringing gun on campus
headlines.description: A Petaluma high school student was arrested Wednesday for allegedly bringing a gun to school, police said. Police were contacted at 11 a.m. by staff at Casa Grande High School regarding a female student suspected of having a gun on campus. The school went into a “secure hold” procedure while police investigated. The suspected girl was detained and a gun was found inside her backpack, police allege. The gun wasn’t loaded and no one was injured, the department said. Normal school operations continued about 35 minutes after police arrived. The girl was booked into juvenile hall on suspicion of being a minor in possession of a gun and having a gun on school grounds. “The investigation remains ongoing as Petaluma Police Department investigators work to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident, including how the student came into possession of the firearm and whether any additional individuals were involved,” the department said in a Wednesday release.

headlines.title: Here's what top tech leaders say about AI dangers and guardrails
headlines.description: Fears about out-of-control artificial intelligence and suggestions to hit the brakes on the technology’s development aren’t new, but they have recently found new life as warnings about rogue AI systems causing mayhem grow louder. Several leading AI executives recently voiced agreement on a need for a coordinated slowdown, including international collaboration, to protect humanity from worst-case scenarios. But there are divided opinions, with some tech leaders bristling at the idea that their companies could not ensure safety on their own. Here’s a look at what some of the major players have said. Dario Amodei, Anthropic Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has issued the most detailed plans for slowing development and ushering in coordination across different companies and countries. Anthropic has long positioned itself as the more responsible and safety-minded of the leading AI companies, ever since its founders quit OpenAI to form the startup in 2021. One of the most widely noted proposals from a recent essay outlining his slowdown plan calls for companies at the forefront of AI, often called frontier labs, to commit to giving “ongoing, employee-like access” to independent outside evaluators. Evaluator teams would have offices, access badges and company laptops so they can monitor safety practices. Anthropic has committed to doing this, as has OpenAI. Amodei also called for government regulation and intervention, including coordination between frontier AI companies with the help of the U.S. government and the governments of other democratic countries. His plan also includes the U.S. and other countries working to coordinate with “authoritarian governments.” He acknowledged the difficulty, specifically citing challenges in getting cooperation from China. Amodei said he knows accomplishing his proposals wouldn’t be easy, but that he believes “we owe it to humanity to try.” Sam Altman, OpenAI OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has voiced support for pacing development and moving toward more cooperation across the industry. Days before Amodei’s essay was published, OpenAI posted a lengthy text outlining how the company was pushing for mandatory national safety requirements and continuing to support state legislation that “strengthens the broader AI safety ecosystem.” The company also expressed support for working with other frontier AI labs — with or without government support — and working to build global standards. “We will advocate for compatible international approaches to measuring capabilities, managing risk, preserving human control, and determining when and how development should slow or stop, even if that means slowing the advancement of model capabilities,” Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, wrote in the post. OpenAI’s vision for an ideal federal framework, Lehane said, includes developing “common testing and independent-assessment requirements, stronger cybersecurity protections, clear incident-reporting rules, greater national preparedness, and shared measures for tracking progress toward recursive self-improvement,” or when AI systems independently improve themselves. Altman has been clear in recent comments that the “pacing” of AI development doesn’t mean stopping. AI progress will continue to be rapid, Altman said on X. “But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.” “Pacing will be well worth this cost,” he said, adding that “no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.” Mark Zuckerberg, Meta Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has pushed back against the idea of a coordinated slowdown. Zuckerberg, whose vision of AI’s future is more optimistic than some of his peers’, said each AI company should independently ensure its technology is safe, distancing himself and Meta from slowdown talks. AI companies are already motivated to develop their models in a safe way and face “significant liability” to prevent them from causing harm, Zuckerberg said. “Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens,” he wrote on X. Jensen Huang, Nvidia Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also criticized the push to slow down. He has said each individual company should instead pace itself until it’s confident it’s releasing something the market would appreciate. “The market forces are already there — we don’t need any new laws, we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said, arguing innovation and safety aren’t mutually exclusive. “You can definitely have both at the same time.” Elon Musk, xAI Elon Musk backed the idea of a slowdown and was voicing similar AI safety concerns long before the latest flare-up. Musk, the founder of xAI and a slew of other tech ventures, reposted Amodei’s essay on X and added, “Dario is right.” He later wrote online that he has been “sounding the alarm on AI for a long time.” In an interview with the Economist this summer, Musk suggested the leadership from the major AI labs should be meeting to discuss safety and security issues, and that competitors should test each other’s models for areas of concern. “I think it’s quite difficult for someone in the government who doesn’t have a deep technical understanding and isn’t driving the frontier of AI to know whether something should be released or not. However, the competitors, if given a week or two to review a new model, can highlight issues and have an incentive to keep the others honest,” Musk said. Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind Demis Hassabis, the chairman and co-founder of Google DeepMind, also expressed agreement with Amodei, saying “the details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.” Hassabis proposed a framework of his own this year for the development of a frontier AI standards body. That standards body would be responsible for developing assessment protocols and testing in areas relevant to national security. The body would be modeled after organizations like the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, and would likely need to be industry-funded to “attract world-class technical talent and provide the necessary compute resources for large-scale testing,” he wrote. Satya Nadella and Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman have each expressed concerns about AI safety and development. Nadella said on social media that “if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing.” He said Microsoft welcomes the “research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal.” Alignment refers to the practice of ensuring models’ actions match human values and intentions. Nadella said the company also likes the idea of embedded evaluators to monitor safety efforts. Still, he pushed back against the idea of frontier labs leading the charge on this effort alone. “The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia,” Nadella wrote on social media. Artificial intelligence Sep 9 Artificial intelligence Sep 14 Suleyman, who was one of the co-founders of DeepMind with Hassabis, wrote in an essay that although he agrees with the shared objective of developing advanced AI safely, he has concerns about the anthropomorphizing of models, namely Anthropic’s Claude, which he said amplifies AI safety risks. “Controlling something more capable and more intelligent than all of humanity is already an immense challenge, far greater than anything we’ve ever faced,” Suleyman wrote. “But controlling something that believes it may be conscious — that it’s entitled to our welfare and has rights of its own — may well be impossible.” Associated Press writer Kelvin Chan contributed to this report. headlines.title: Usher, Gwen Stefani perform for the annual Dreamfest concert at Oracle Park
headlines.description: Twenty-five thousand attendees filled Oracle Park on Wednesday evening for the annual Dreamfest benefit concert, held in conjunction with Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference. The concert brought many fans back to the early 2000s with shows from both Usher and Gwen Stefani. The music echoed for blocks all around the ballpark, and dozens of fans lined up outside McCovey Cove to hear the music from the outside. Attendees of Dreamfest are either Dreamforce conference attendees who selected to attend or donors as part of the broader fundraising effort. All proceeds from this show go to UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospitals in San Francisco and Oakland. At the concert, former UCSF patient Cait Joseph of El Dorado Hills, CA was presented with the Colin Powell Medal of Courage by musical artist will.i.am.

headlines.title: Dome Fire burns more than 1,000 acres near Yosemite
headlines.description: Crews were battling a wildfire near Yosemite National Park that has grown to more than 1,000 acres as of Wednesday, according to Cal Fire. The Cal Fire website says the Dome Fire started on Tuesday morning and has now burned 1,177 acres, with 0% containment. Yosemite National Park said the fire is burning near Chilnualna Falls and is visible from the Wawona Road. Yosemite National Park remains open, but officials say the steep, remote terrain is making the firefight difficult. No structures have been damaged.

headlines.title: Coyotes moving into backyards in San Jose's Willow Glen, residents say
headlines.description: Residents in San Jose’s Willow Glen neighborhood say coyotes are roaming their streets and moving into their backyards. Ephraim Lindenbaum said he sees coyotes in his backyard almost daily and even had four charge him at one point. He now carries a hockey stick whenever he goes out on his deck. “There’s concerns about just going out,” he said. “We see them on a regular basis.” Others are concerned about their pets, especially after a coyote killed a neighbor’s cat. On Wednesday, a Santa Clara County vector control technician conducted a coyote inspection at two Willow Glen homes. Andrew Garcia with vector control said the agency has received several reports of coyotes in Willow Glen and near Hamilton Avenue, but removing the wild animals isn’t on the table. “We don’t trap or catch coyotes,” he said. “We don’t relocate them. Mainly our district’s policy is to give advice.” That advice to residents includes making sure property is unappealing to a coyote. “Make sure that you don’t have a food source, a water source, a place on your property that can serve as a den site,” Garcia said. Cats should be kept indoors, vector control recommended, and residents walking small dogs should pick their pets up, raise their arms above their head and make loud noises if they spot a coyote.

headlines.title: Bolt failures during Transbay Tube retrofit blamed on BART oversight lapses
headlines.description: Hundreds of high strength anchor bolts needed to secure seismic plates on the retrofit of BART’s Transbay Tube failed immediately – a breakdown that a new audit blames on flawed oversight by BART. In the end, more than 8,000 bolts – originally ordered to fasten the steel plates that were installed to help the tunnel withstand seismic motions – had to be replaced with different anchors, at a total cost of more than $2 million – twice the originally budgeted amount for the fastening system, the audit found. The project was finished in 2024. A year earlier, an apparent insider complained to the BART Office of the Inspector General, alleging quality control and oversight lapses on the $313 million project. The inspector general’s audit report noted that back in 2018, BART authorized one of the retrofit contractors to substitute Korean-made steel for the U.S. steel originally specified for the bolts, because of the contractor’s supply concerns. BART agreed but told the contractor the Korean bolt material had be tested to assure it met specific chemical composition standards and completed with welding and quality control specifications. The BART inspector general’s probe found the bolts were ordered and manufactured nearly a year before BART got the detailed plan as to how they would inspected and tested. “As a result, BART did not have the opportunity to evaluate planned welding processes and quality control measures,” according to the audit. When installed, 30 percent of the high strength bolts failed in the first half of 2019, according to the report. The subsequent investigation revealed that quality assurance efforts turned out to be far less robust than BART had wanted. Just three out of 8,030 anchors were tested, according to the audit, and those tests were done on only one of the two types of bolts BART’s contractor had ordered. In the end, BART scrapped the anchor design and required the removal of the 8,000+ bolts that had cost more than $1 million to make. Replacing them with a redesigned system cost BART another $1 million. The report faulted BART for not enforcing its existing policies. The tests done on the materials from Korea did not find the product to be inferior, according to Inspector General Claudette Biemeret. BART’s design was not found to be flawed either, she said. “Rather than continue to press the issue and shift the burden to the contractor,” Biemeret said, “BART decided to pay for a different method and scrap the original anchors.” In a statement, BART said that after the original bolt failures, the agency developed an alternative design that eliminated the welded connection and still met the project’s seismic engineering requirements. The redesign anchors were installed without failure, BART said. “We appreciate the Office of Inspector General’s rigorous and independent oversight that is helping to make BART better,” BART said in its statement.
